title: Frattini Subgroups and the Burnside Basis Theorem

items.title: The Frattini subgroup of a finite group is characteristic
items.strategy: Every automorphism sends maximal proper subgroups to maximal proper subgroups, hence permutes the family whose intersection is $\Phi(G)$. Taking the image of that intersection gives the same intersection. Treat the trivial group through the published empty-intersection convention.

items.title: Generation of a finite group is detected modulo its Frattini subgroup
items.strategy: The forward implication follows by applying the quotient map. Conversely, generation of the quotient gives $G=\langle S\rangle\Phi(G)$. Since $G$ is finite, list the finitely many elements of $\Phi(G)$ adjoined to $S$ and remove them one at a time using the nongenerator characterization. The trivial group and $S=\varnothing$ are included.

items.title: Elementary abelian $p$-groups
An elementary abelian $p$-group has a canonical $\mathbb F_p$-vector-space structure
items.strategy: For $\bar a\in\mathbb Z/p$ and $x\in E$, define $\bar a\cdot x=x^a$. Exponent $p$ makes this independent of the representative, commutativity converts addition of scalars into multiplication in $E$, and the group power laws verify the remaining scalar axioms. Conversely the additive group of any finite $\mathbb F_p$-linear structure is elementary abelian. State the zero group and the scalars $0,1$ explicitly.

items.title: $\mathbb F_p$-spanning sets, independence, and bases in an elementary abelian $p$-group
Finite elementary abelian $p$-groups have bases, basis extension, and a well-defined dimension
items.strategy: Starting from a finite spanning set, delete redundant elements until a basis remains; starting from an independent set, adjoin elements outside its span until it spans. For any basis $B$, unique coordinates give a bijection $(\mathbb Z/p)^B\to E$, so $|E|=p^{|B|}$ and unique prime factorization makes all basis sizes equal. The empty basis handles $E=1$ without a choice principle.

items.title: The $p$th-power subgroup $G^p$
The Frattini quotient is the largest elementary abelian quotient of a finite $p$-group
items.strategy: Every maximal subgroup of the finite $p$-group is normal of index $p$, so every commutator and every $p$th power lies in their intersection; hence $P/\Phi(P)$ is elementary abelian. If $N\trianglelefteq P$ and $P/N$ is elementary abelian, extend each nonzero coset to a finite basis, omit that basis vector to obtain a maximal subgroup of $P/N$, and pull it back. The intersection of these pullbacks is $N$, so $\Phi(P)\le N$. Include $P=1$, $N=P$, and both directions of the equivalence.

items.title: $\Phi(P)=P'P^p$ for a finite $p$-group
items.strategy: First show that $P^p$ is characteristic and hence normal; $P'$ is normal, so $P'P^p$ is a normal subgroup. The elementary-abelian Frattini quotient kills commutators and $p$th powers, giving $P'P^p\le\Phi(P)$. Conversely $P/P'P^p$ is abelian of exponent $p$, so the largest-elementary-abelian-quotient theorem gives $\Phi(P)\le P'P^p$. Check the trivial group and $p=2$.

items.title: If $H\le P$ are finite $p$-groups, then $\Phi(H)\le\Phi(P)$
items.strategy: Apply the Frattini formula to both groups. Every commutator of elements of $H$ is a commutator in $P$, and every $p$th power from $H$ is a $p$th power from $P$, so $H'H^p\le P'P^p$. Include $H=1$ and $H=P$.

items.title: $\Phi(P/N)=\Phi(P)N/N$ for a normal subgroup of a finite $p$-group
items.strategy: Under the quotient map, commutators map onto $(P/N)'$ and $p$th powers map onto $(P/N)^p$. Apply the Frattini formula on both sides and the quotient group laws to obtain $(P/N)'(P/N)^p=P'P^pN/N$. Check $N=1$, $N=P$, and equality in both inclusions.

items.title: $\Phi(P\times Q)=\Phi(P)\times\Phi(Q)$ for finite $p$-groups
items.strategy: Compute commutators and $p$th powers componentwise in the external direct product: $(P\times Q)'=P'\times Q'$ and $(P\times Q)^p=P^p\times Q^p$. The Frattini formula then gives the equality. Include a trivial factor and the product of two trivial groups.

items.title: $\Phi(P)=P^2$ for a finite $2$-group
items.strategy: The quotient $P/P^2$ has exponent at most two, and every group of exponent two is abelian by expanding $(xy)^2=1$. Hence $P'\le P^2$, and the Frattini formula reduces to $\Phi(P)=P'P^2=P^2$. The trivial group is included.

items.title: A finite $p$-group has trivial Frattini subgroup exactly when it is elementary abelian
items.strategy: If $\Phi(P)=1$, the Frattini quotient theorem identifies $P$ itself as elementary abelian. Conversely, if $P$ is elementary abelian, the quotient by $1$ is elementary abelian, so the minimal-kernel clause gives $\Phi(P)\le1$. Treat $P=1$ and both directions explicitly.

items.title: Minimal generating sets of a group
The generator rank $d(P)$ of a finite $p$-group
Burnside Basis Theorem
items.strategy: Generation of $P$ is equivalent to spanning $P/\Phi(P)$ by the generation-detection corollary. An inclusion-minimal generating set has distinct quotient images and maps bijectively to an inclusion-minimal spanning set, hence to a basis. Conversely, if the quotient map restricts to a bijection from $X$ onto a basis, then $X$ generates and removing any member destroys spanning and therefore generation. State this restricted-bijection clause explicitly so two distinct lifts of one basis vector are not misclassified. Handle $P=1$ with the empty basis.

items.title: Minimal generating sets of a finite $p$-group have size $d(P)$
items.strategy: Burnside basis sends every minimal generating set to a basis, whose size is $d(P)$. Given any generating set, its image spans the Frattini quotient; delete redundant images until a basis remains and lift the corresponding subset. The empty generating set for the trivial group gives size zero.

items.title: Every element outside $\Phi(P)$ belongs to a minimal generating set of $P$
items.strategy: The image of $x\notin\Phi(P)$ is nonzero and hence is a one-element independent set in the Frattini quotient. Extend it to a finite basis without choice, lift the other basis vectors, and apply Burnside basis. Explain why the statement is vacuous for $P=1$.

items.title: A nontrivial finite $p$-group is cyclic exactly when $d(P)=1$
items.strategy: If $d(P)=1$, lift a one-element basis and use Burnside basis to obtain one generator. Conversely, a generator maps to a spanning singleton, so the nonzero Frattini quotient has basis size one. Nontriviality excludes the zero-dimensional quotient; record separately that $d(1)=0$.

items.title: Maximal subgroups of a finite $p$-group are the inverse images of Frattini hyperplanes
items.strategy: Correspondence sends each maximal subgroup $M$ to a maximal proper subgroup of the finite elementary abelian group $P/\Phi(P)$. Extend a basis of that subgroup by one vector to see that it has codimension one and is the kernel of the coordinate homomorphism to $\mathbb Z/p$; conversely the kernel of any nonzero linear homomorphism is a hyperplane whose inverse image is maximal. Treat $P=1$ and the one-dimensional quotient.

items.title: Automorphisms act linearly on the Frattini quotient
items.strategy: Characteristicity of $\Phi(P)$ lets each automorphism of $P$ induce an automorphism of $P/\Phi(P)$. The identity $\alpha(x^a)=\alpha(x)^a$ makes the induced map preserve the canonical $\mathbb F_p$-scalar action. Verify that composition is preserved, obtaining a homomorphism $\rho_P$ from $\operatorname{Aut}(P)$ to the group of $\mathbb F_p$-linear automorphisms of the quotient, including $P=1$.

items.title: Hall–Burnside: coprime automorphisms are detected on the Frattini quotient
items.strategy: Assume a nontrivial $p'$-subgroup $A\le\operatorname{Aut}(P)$ acts trivially on $P/\Phi(P)$. Cauchy's theorem gives an element $\alpha$ of prime order $q\ne p$. It preserves every Frattini coset; the cyclic $q$-group acts on each coset, whose $p$-power size is not divisible by $q$, so each coset has an $\alpha$-fixed representative. Choose fixed representatives of a basis of the quotient, apply Burnside basis, and conclude that $\alpha$ fixes a generating set and is the identity, a contradiction. Include $P=1$ and $A=1$.

items.title: The kernel of the automorphism action on $P/\Phi(P)$ is a $p$-group
items.strategy: The kernel is finite because it is a subgroup of the permutations of finite $P$. If a prime $q\ne p$ divided its order, Cauchy's theorem would produce an order-$q$ subgroup acting trivially on the Frattini quotient, contradicting Hall–Burnside. Unique prime factorization therefore makes the kernel order a power of $p$. Include the trivial kernel and $P=1$.

items.title: Sylow $p$-subgroups of a finite group
The number $n_p(G)$ of Sylow $p$-subgroups
Maximal proper subgroups
$p$-complements in finite groups
The $p$-core $O_p(G)$ as the largest normal $p$-subgroup
The Fitting subgroup $F(G)=\prod_p O_p(G)$ of a finite group
The Frattini subgroup $\Phi(G)$ as the intersection of the maximal subgroups of a finite group
The centralizer $C_G(H)$ of a subgroup
The centralizer of a normal subgroup is normal
items.strategy: Conjugate a centralizing element and use normality of $N$ to move the conjugating pair past $n$; then apply the inclusion to $g^{-1}$ for the reverse containment.

items.title: A nontrivial normal subgroup of a solvable group contains a nontrivial abelian subgroup normal in the whole group
items.strategy: Take the last nontrivial term of the derived series of $N$; it is abelian by construction and characteristic in $N$, hence normal in $Q$.

items.title: If $|G|=p^a m$ with $p\nmid m$, then $v_p\binom{p^a m}{p^a}=0$
items.strategy: Apply the valuation to the identity \(\binom{p^am}{p^a}(p^a)!= (p^am)^{\underline{p^a}}\). For each \(0<j<p^a\), prove \(v_p(p^am-j)=v_p(j)\); the remaining factor contributes \(a+v_p(m)=a\), so cancellation leaves valuation zero. Check \(a=0\) separately and never apply the valuation to zero.

items.title: Sylow I: every finite group has a Sylow $p$-subgroup
items.strategy: Use strong induction on \(|G|\) and Wielandt's left action on the \(p^a\)-element subsets of \(G\). The valuation lemma makes the total number of subsets prime to \(p\), so one orbit has index prime to \(p\); its stabilizer has the full \(p\)-part of \(|G|\) and is proper unless \(G\) itself is a \(p\)-group. Apply induction to that stabilizer. Include \(a=0\), the trivial group, and the case \(m=1\).

items.title: Sylow II: every $p$-subgroup lies in a conjugate of any Sylow $p$-subgroup, and the Sylow $p$-subgroups form a single conjugacy class
items.strategy: The Statement has two clauses and BOTH are asserted, because the second is what every later item on this page actually cites. Clause (a), containment: let a finite \(p\)-subgroup \(H\) act by left multiplication on \(G/P\) for a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup \(P\). The set \(G/P\) has cardinality prime to \(p\), so the fixed-point congruence gives a fixed coset \(gP\), and the fixed-coset condition is exactly \(H\le gPg^{-1}\). Clause (b), conjugacy: apply clause (a) with \(H=Q\) a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup; then \(Q\le gPg^{-1}\) and \(|Q|=|gPg^{-1}|=p^a\) is finite, so \(Q=gPg^{-1}\). Hence conjugation acts transitively on the set of Sylow \(p\)-subgroups. Treat the trivial \(p\)-subgroup and primes not dividing \(|G|\).

items.title: Sylow III*: $n_p(G)=[G:N_G(P)]$
items.strategy: Conjugation is transitive on the Sylow \(p\)-subgroups by Sylow II, and the stabilizer of \(P\) is exactly \(N_G(P)\). Apply orbit–stabiliser, including the unique/trivial Sylow case.

items.title: Sylow III: $n_p\equiv1\pmod p$ and $n_p\mid m$ when $|G|=p^a m$ with $p\nmid m$
items.strategy: Let a Sylow subgroup \(P\) act by conjugation on the Sylow set. If \(P\) fixes \(Q\), then \(P,Q\le N_G(Q)\), and Sylow II inside that normalizer forces \(P=Q\); hence there is exactly one fixed point and the congruence follows. The normalizer-index formula and \(P\le N_G(P)\) give \(n_p\mid m\).

items.title: A Sylow $p$-subgroup is normal if and only if it is unique
items.strategy: A normal Sylow subgroup is fixed by every conjugation, and Sylow II says every Sylow subgroup is one of its conjugates. Conversely, uniqueness makes the subgroup conjugation-invariant.

items.title: A subgroup containing the normalizer of a Sylow subgroup is self-normalizing
items.strategy: For \(N_G(P)\le H\le G\) and \(x\in N_G(H)\), the groups \(P\) and \(xPx^{-1}\) are Sylow in \(H\). Conjugate them inside \(H\); the resulting element puts \(x\) in \(H\). Specialize to \(H=N_G(P)\) to obtain \(N_G(N_G(P))=N_G(P)\).

items.title: Frattini argument: if $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $P$ is Sylow in $N$, then $G=N N_G(P)$
items.strategy: For each \(g\in G\), normality makes \(gPg^{-1}\) Sylow in \(N\). Sylow II inside \(N\) supplies \(n\in N\) conjugating it back to \(P\), so \(ng\in N_G(P)\) and \(g\in N N_G(P)\). The reverse containment is immediate.

items.title: A normal Sylow subgroup of a normal subgroup is normal in the whole group
items.strategy: A unique Sylow subgroup is preserved by every automorphism of its ambient normal subgroup, so it is characteristic there; characteristic-in-normal gives normality in the whole group.

items.title: Every proper subgroup of a finite nilpotent group is properly contained in its normalizer
items.strategy: Use a central series and take the first term not contained in the proper subgroup \(H\). The preceding term lies in \(H\), so an element newly appearing at that stage normalizes \(H\) modulo the preceding term but is not in \(H\). Include \(H=1\) and class zero.

items.title: Maximal subgroups of finite nilpotent groups are normal of prime index
items.strategy: The normalizer condition and maximality force \(N_G(M)=G\), hence \(M\trianglelefteq G\). The quotient has no nontrivial proper subgroup; Cauchy's theorem then forces its nontrivial order to be prime. Check that a maximal subgroup is proper and that the quotient is nontrivial.

items.title: Every nontrivial finite $p$-group has a normal subgroup of index $p$
items.strategy: In the finite nonempty collection of proper subgroups choose one maximal by inclusion. The nilpotent maximal-subgroup theorem makes its index prime, while Lagrange makes that index divide a power of \(p\), so it is \(p\). This produces the subgroup before invoking the already-published theorem that any index-\(p\) subgroup of a finite \(p\)-group is normal.

items.title: Distinct normal Sylow subgroups centralize one another
items.strategy: For normal Sylow \(p\)- and \(q\)-subgroups with \(p\ne q\), every commutator lies in their intersection. Lagrange makes that intersection trivial because its order divides coprime prime powers.

items.title: A finite group is nilpotent if and only if all Sylow subgroups are normal, if and only if it is their internal direct product
items.strategy: If \(G\) is nilpotent and \(P\) is Sylow, self-normalization of \(N_G(P)\) contradicts the normalizer condition unless \(N_G(P)=G\). Normal Sylow subgroups for distinct primes commute and have trivial intersections; their product has order \(|G|\), so it is the internal direct product. Conversely each factor is a finite \(p\)-group and hence nilpotent, and a finite direct product of nilpotent groups is nilpotent. Include the trivial group and the one-prime case.

items.title: A finite product of normal $p$-subgroups is a normal $p$-subgroup
items.strategy: Induct on the finite family. For two normal \(p\)-subgroups \(A,B\), the product is a normal subgroup and \(|AB|=|A||B|/|A\cap B|\) is a power of \(p\). Include the empty product and repeated factors.

items.title: The Fitting subgroup is nilpotent and is the largest normal nilpotent subgroup of a finite group
items.strategy: The product of the \(p\)-cores is an internal direct product, hence nilpotent. If \(N\trianglelefteq G\) is nilpotent, each of its unique Sylow subgroups is characteristic in \(N\), hence normal in \(G\), so it lies in the corresponding \(p\)-core. Their product contains \(N\). Handle \(G=1\) with the empty product.

items.title: Philip Hall: in a finite solvable group the Fitting subgroup contains its own centralizer
items.strategy: Suppose $C=C_G(F)\not\le F$. Then $CF/F$ is a nontrivial normal subgroup of the solvable group $G/F$, so it contains a nontrivial abelian $A/F$ normal in $G/F$. The Dedekind law gives $A=F(C\cap A)$, and $C\cap A$ has its derived subgroup inside $Z(C\cap A)$, hence is normal nilpotent and lies in $F$ — forcing $A\le F$, a contradiction.

items.title: The Frattini subgroup consists exactly of the nongenerators of a finite group
items.strategy: If \(x\notin\Phi(G)\), a maximal subgroup omitting \(x\) shows that adjoining \(x\) can enlarge a generating set. Conversely, if \(\langle S,x\rangle=G\) while \(\langle S\rangle\ne G\), extend the latter finite subgroup to a maximal subgroup; it contains \(S\) but cannot contain \(x\). Treat the trivial group, whose empty intersection convention gives \(\Phi(1)=1\).

items.title: Nilpotence lifts over the Frattini subgroup of a finite group
items.strategy: Assume \(\Phi(G)\le N\trianglelefteq G\) and \(N/\Phi(G)\) is nilpotent. For a Sylow subgroup \(P\) of \(N\), its image is the unique Sylow subgroup of the quotient, so \(P\Phi(G)\trianglelefteq G\). Apply the Frattini argument to \(P\le P\Phi(G)\) to get \(G=N_G(P)\Phi(G)\); the nongenerator property forces \(N_G(P)=G\). Thus every Sylow subgroup of \(N\) is normal and \(N\) is nilpotent. Record the special equivalence for \(N=G\).

items.title: The Frattini subgroup of a finite group is nilpotent
items.strategy: Apply the lifting theorem with \(N=\Phi(G)\); its quotient by \(\Phi(G)\) is the trivial nilpotent group. Include \(G=1\).

items.title: The Frattini subgroup is contained in the Fitting subgroup
items.strategy: The Frattini subgroup is characteristic, hence normal, and is nilpotent; maximality of the Fitting subgroup gives the inclusion.

items.title: $F(G/\Phi(G))=F(G)/\Phi(G)$ for every finite group
items.strategy: The image \(F(G)/\Phi(G)\) is normal and nilpotent, giving one inclusion. For the reverse inclusion, pull \(F(G/\Phi(G))\) back to a normal subgroup \(N\) of \(G\); the lifting theorem makes \(N\) nilpotent, so \(N\le F(G)\). Check the trivial quotient.

items.title: Sylow and maximal-subgroup characterizations of finite nilpotence
items.strategy: Combine the three Sylow/direct-product equivalences with the maximal-subgroup clause. If every maximal subgroup is normal, the diagonal map \(G/\Phi(G)\to\prod_M G/M\) is injective; each quotient has prime order, so the product and its subgroup are nilpotent. Lift nilpotence through \(\Phi(G)\). The reverse direction is the maximal-subgroup theorem. Include a finite group with no maximal subgroups, necessarily the trivial group.

items.title: For prime $p$, $|\operatorname{Aut}((\mathbb Z/p)\times(\mathbb Z/p))|=(p^2-1)(p^2-p)$
items.strategy: Put \(E_p=(\mathbb Z/p,+)\times(\mathbb Z/p,+)\) and let \(e_1=(1,0)\), \(e_2=(0,1)\). A homomorphism \(E_p\to E_p\) is determined by the ordered pair \(u=f(e_1),v=f(e_2)\), since multiplication by a residue class is repeated addition. Prove that it is an automorphism exactly when \(u\ne0\) and \(v\notin\langle u\rangle\): field division gives injectivity, and an injective self-map of the finite set \(E_p\) is bijective. There are \(p^2-1\) choices for \(u\), the subgroup \(\langle u\rangle\) has \(p\) elements, and then there are \(p^2-p\) choices for \(v\). Check \(p=2\) directly. A Remark may record that this group is conventionally written \(GL_2(\mathbb F_p)\); that is a name only, since matrices are defined on a later page, so assert no isomorphism to a matrix group and cite no matrix item.

items.title: Every group of order $p^2q$ for distinct primes has a normal Sylow subgroup
items.strategy: If \(p>q\), the restrictions \(n_p\mid q\) and \(n_p\equiv1\pmod p\) force \(n_p=1\). If \(q>p\), then \(n_q\in\{1,p^2\}\); the second value forces \(q\mid(p-1)(p+1)\), hence the sole exceptional pair \((p,q)=(2,3)\). For order \(12\), if the four Sylow \(3\)-subgroups are nonnormal, their eight nonidentity elements leave exactly four elements, so every Sylow \(2\)-subgroup is that same four-element complement and is normal. Keep the two prime orderings and the order-twelve boundary case explicit.

items.title: No group of order $p^2q$ for distinct primes is simple
items.strategy: The normal Sylow subgroup supplied by the theorem has prime-power order strictly between one and \(p^2q\), so it is a nontrivial proper normal subgroup.

items.title: Every group of order $30$ has normal Sylow $3$- and $5$-subgroups and is not simple
items.strategy: Choose an involution by Cauchy's theorem and use the left regular permutation representation. Left multiplication by the involution is a product of fifteen transpositions, so composing with sign gives a surjection to \({\pm1}\) whose normal kernel has order \(15\). The published order-\(pq\) classification makes that kernel cyclic. Its Sylow \(3\)- and \(5\)-subgroups are normal in the kernel and hence normal in \(G\). Either is a nontrivial proper normal subgroup.

items.title: Every group of order $105$ has normal Sylow $5$- and $7$-subgroups and is not simple
items.strategy: The nonunique counts \(n_5=21\) and \(n_7=15\) would already contribute \(84+90\) distinct nonidentity elements, so at least one of the two Sylow subgroups is normal. Multiply it by a Sylow subgroup for the other prime to obtain a subgroup \(H\) of order \(35\). The action on the three left cosets has kernel \(K\subseteq H\); the first isomorphism theorem gives \([G:K]\mid6\), while \([G:K]\mid105\) and \(3=[G:H]\mid[G:K]\), so \(K=H\) and \(H\trianglelefteq G\). The order-\(pq\) classification makes \(H\) cyclic, and its normal Sylow \(5\)- and \(7\)-subgroups are therefore normal in \(G\).

items.title: There are exactly two isomorphism classes of groups of order $105$
items.strategy: Let \(N_5\) and \(N_7\) be the normal Sylow subgroups and choose a Sylow \(3\)-subgroup \(P\). Then \(H=N_7P\) has order \(21\) and \(G=N_5H\). Conjugation gives \(H\to\operatorname{Aut}(N_5)\); its image has order dividing both \(21\) and \(4=|\operatorname{Aut}(C_5)|\), so it is trivial. Hence \(G\cong C_5\times H\). The published order-\(pq\) classification gives exactly two choices for \(H\), one cyclic and one nonabelian; their products with \(C_5\) remain distinguished by commutativity. In the cyclic case, pair a generator of \(N_5\) with a generator of \(H\): the order of that pair is \(\operatorname{lcm}(5,21)=105\), so the abelian type is cyclic of order \(105\), hence \(C_{105}\). Check the chosen subgroups have trivial intersections and that no third isomorphism type is introduced.

items.title: Every group of order $45$ is abelian
items.strategy: Sylow III forces both the order-nine and order-five Sylow subgroups to be unique. They commute, their product is the whole group, and both factors are abelian, so the internal direct product is abelian.

items.title: No group of order $pq$ for distinct primes is simple
items.strategy: Order the primes as \(p<q\). The published order-\(pq\) lemma supplies a normal subgroup of order \(q\), which is nontrivial and proper.

items.title: False statement: every divisor of the order of a finite group occurs as a subgroup order
items.strategy: State the abelian converse and Sylow's prime-power partial converse, then construct \(A_4\) natively and show a hypothetical subgroup of order six would have index two and hence be normal, contradicting the conjugacy structure of its three-cycles. Record agreement with the published B-page witness without citing it.

items.title: False statement: all subgroups of the same $p$-power order are conjugate
items.strategy: In \(S_4\), the order-two subgroups generated by \((12)\) and \((12)(34)\) cannot be conjugate because their nonidentity generators have different cycle types. Contrast this with Sylow II, which concerns only subgroups of maximal \(p\)-power order.

items.title: False statement: one unique Sylow subgroup forces the whole group to be a direct product
items.strategy: Use the nonabelian group \(C_q\rtimes C_p\) when \(p\mid q-1\). Its Sylow \(q\)-subgroup is unique and normal, but the defining action is nontrivial, so the semidirect product is not direct.

items.title: False statement: every group of order $42$ has a normal Sylow $2$-subgroup
items.strategy: Construct the affine group \(\mathbb F_7\rtimes\mathbb F_7^\times\) of order \(42\). Its seven involutions \(x\mapsto -x+b\) generate seven Sylow \(2\)-subgroups, so none is normal. Check directly that the translation subgroup is the normal Sylow \(7\)-subgroup.

items.title: False statement: finite nilpotent groups and finite solvable groups are the same
items.strategy: The forward implication is published. For the converse, compute \(S_3' = A_3\) and \(A_3'=1\), while its three Sylow \(2\)-subgroups are not normal; the Sylow characterization therefore makes \(S_3\) solvable but not nilpotent.

title: Semidirect Products, Automorphism Groups and Split Extensions
note: frontier-13 R2.1 (2026-08-15, group A recommendation): added the published order-52 page polynomial-rings-and-roots so the root-bound lemma cites the published theorem instead of re-deriving coefficient arrays inline. Verified published, order 52 < 68, absent from the prior closure (26 -> 31), 0 seams across all 11 run pairs, no new redundant-prereq warning. Approved on citational accuracy: citing a published theorem beats an inline re-derivation.

items.title: An action of a group $H$ on a group $N$ by automorphisms
The external semidirect product $N\rtimes_\alpha H$
The semidirect-product multiplication makes $N\times H$ a group
items.strategy: Expand both parenthesisations and use that $\alpha$ is a homomorphism into automorphisms. Verify identity $(1,1)$ and the formula $(n,h)^{-1}=(\alpha(h^{-1})(n^{-1}),h^{-1})$.

items.title: The canonical copy of $N$ is normal, the canonical copy of $H$ is a complement, and conjugation induces the action
items.strategy: Embed $N$ as $(n,1)$ and $H$ as $(1,h)$. Calculate normality, trivial intersection, unique factorisation, and the conjugation formula.

items.title: The canonical semidirect decomposition is an internal direct product if and only if the defining action is trivial
items.strategy: A trivial action makes multiplication coordinatewise. Conversely, if the complement is normal, its commutator with the normal factor lies in both factors and is trivial, so conjugation fixes $N$.

items.title: An internal semidirect product and a complement to a normal subgroup
Recognition theorem: $G=NH$ with $N\trianglelefteq G$, $N\cap H=1$ exactly realises an external semidirect product
items.strategy: Conjugation by $H$ restricts to automorphisms of $N$. The map $(n,h)\mapsto nh$ respects multiplication, is onto by $G=NH$, and is one-to-one by the trivial intersection. The canonical-factor proposition gives the converse.

items.title: Group extensions, sections, complements, and split extensions
Splitting lemma for groups: a section, a complement, and a semidirect-product decomposition are equivalent
items.strategy: The image of a homomorphic section intersects the kernel trivially and multiplies with it to all of the middle group, so it is a complement and recognition gives a semidirect product. Conversely, a complement makes the quotient map restrict to an isomorphism whose inverse is a section. The canonical factors of an external semidirect product supply the remaining implication.

items.title: The quaternion group $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ inside the nonzero quaternions
$Q_8$ is a subgroup of $\mathbb{H}^{\times}$ with eight elements, and $-1$ is its only element of order $2$
The outer automorphism group $\operatorname{Out}(G)=\operatorname{Aut}(G)/\operatorname{Inn}(G)$
If $K$ is characteristic in $N$ and $N$ is normal in $G$, then $K$ is normal in $G$
items.strategy: Conjugation by each element of $G$ restricts to an automorphism of $N$; characteristicity makes that restriction preserve $K$, which is exactly normality in $G$.

items.title: The holomorph $\operatorname{Hol}(G)=G\rtimes\operatorname{Aut}(G)$
The holomorph acts faithfully on $G$ by affine permutations $x\mapsto g\alpha(x)$
items.strategy: Check that composition matches holomorph multiplication. If an affine permutation is the identity, evaluate at the group identity to get $g=1$, then conclude $\alpha$ fixes every element.

items.title: A permutation group with a regular normal subgroup $G$ embeds in $\operatorname{Hol}(G)$
items.strategy: Identify the regular normal subgroup with the left translations of $G$. Every permutation factors uniquely as a left translation followed by a stabiliser element. Normality shows that a stabiliser element conjugates left translation by $g$ to left translation by its value at $g$, so its restriction is an automorphism of $G$; the factorisation therefore lands faithfully in the holomorph.

items.title: $\operatorname{Aut}(C_n)\cong(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times$
items.strategy: An endomorphism is determined by $g\mapsto g^a$ and is invertible exactly when $g^a$ is a generator, equivalently $\gcd(a,n)=1$. Composition multiplies residue classes. Include $n=1$.

items.title: $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb Z^n)\cong GL_n(\mathbb Z)$ for every finite rank $n$
items.strategy: Expand each basis image in the free basis. The universal property identifies homomorphisms with integer coefficient arrays, and a finite-sum calculation makes composition matrix multiplication. Invertibility on both sides agrees. Include $n=0$ and define the pre-matrix notation explicitly rather than citing the later matrix page.

items.title: Actions changed by automorphisms of the kernel and complement give isomorphic semidirect products
items.strategy: Under the standard compatibility between two actions and automorphisms of both factors, verify the coordinatewise comparison map respects multiplication; construct its inverse from the inverse automorphisms.

items.title: The generalized dihedral group $\operatorname{Dih}(A)=A\rtimes C_2$ for an abelian group $A$
The dihedral group of order $2n$ is $C_n\rtimes C_2$ with inversion action
items.strategy: Specialize to $A=C_n$. The canonical generators satisfy $r^n=s^2=1$ and $srs^{-1}=r^{-1}$, and every element has a unique form $r^i$ or $r^is$.

items.title: For prime $q$ and $d\ge1$, the congruence $x^d\equiv1\pmod q$ has at most $d$ residue-class solutions
items.strategy: The prime modulus makes $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ a field and hence an integral domain. View the solutions as the roots in that domain of the nonzero degree-$d$ polynomial $X^d-1$, using equality of residue classes to translate the displayed congruence. Apply the published root bound for polynomials over an integral domain.

items.title: If $p<q$ are primes and $|G|=pq$, then $G$ has a normal subgroup of order $q$
items.strategy: Cauchy supplies $Q$ of order $q$. Act on its $p$ left cosets. The kernel lies in $Q$, while the image order divides both $pq$ and $p!$. Since $q>p$, the kernel order is divisible by $q$, hence the kernel is $Q$ and $Q$ is normal.

items.title: For primes $p<q$, nontrivial actions of $C_p$ on $C_q$ exist exactly when $p\mid(q-1)$ and are unique up to automorphisms
items.strategy: Identify $\operatorname{Aut}(C_q)$ with the abelian group $U(q)$ of order $q-1$. A nontrivial map from $C_p$ is injective; existence follows from Cauchy when $p\mid q-1$. Two distinct order-$p$ subgroups intersect trivially, so their union already contains $2p-1>p$ solutions to $x^p=1$, contradicting the root bound. Reparametrise the source generator for uniqueness.

items.title: Classification of groups of order $pq$ for primes $p<q$
items.strategy: Choose $P,Q$ of orders $p,q$; $Q$ is normal, their intersection is trivial, and $QP=G$, so $G\cong C_q\rtimes C_p$. For the trivial action, generators of the two commuting factors have a product of order $pq$: a power equal to one forces both $p$ and $q$ to divide its exponent. If $p\nmid q-1$ only this cyclic type occurs; if $p\mid q-1$ there is also one nonabelian type. Distinguish the two types by commutativity.

title: Composition Series, the Jordan–Hölder Theorem and Solvable Groups

items.title: Subnormal and normal series, factors, refinements, and equivalence
Composition series, composition factors, and composition length
Every finite group has a composition series
items.strategy: Induct on |G|. The trivial group gives the length-zero case. For nontrivial finite G, choose a proper normal subgroup N of maximum cardinality (possibly 1), prove G/N is simple by correspondence, take a composition series of N by induction, and append G. This finite maximization uses no choice principle.

items.title: Dedekind's modular law for subgroup products
items.strategy: For A≤C and B≤G such that AB is a subgroup, prove A(B∩C)=AB∩C by the two inclusions: the forward inclusion is immediate, while x=ab∈AB∩C has b=a^{-1}x∈B∩C. State explicitly that the hypothesis ensuring AB is a subgroup cannot be omitted.

items.title: The Zassenhaus butterfly lemma
items.strategy: For A◁A* and B◁B*, set X=A(A*∩B), X*=A(A*∩B*), Y=(A∩B*)B, and Y*=(A*∩B*)B. Verify X◁X* and Y◁Y* by conjugation and the modular law. Put D=(A∩B*)(A*∩B), use the second isomorphism and correspondence theorems on A*∩B*, and identify both quotients with (A*∩B*)/D to obtain X*/X≅Y*/Y.

items.title: The Schreier refinement theorem
items.strategy: Given subnormal series G=G_0▷⋯▷G_m=1 and G=H_0▷⋯▷H_n=1, refine the interval G_i▷G_{i+1} by G_{i+1}(G_i∩H_j) and refine H_j▷H_{j+1} symmetrically by H_{j+1}(G_i∩H_j). Prove each is a subnormal chain and use the butterfly lemma cell-by-cell to pair its mn factors after deleting repetitions.

items.title: The Jordan–Hölder theorem for groups
items.strategy: Apply Schreier refinement to two composition series. A refinement of a composition series can insert only repeated adjacent terms because each original factor is simple; deleting repetitions therefore recovers the original series. Conclude equal length and a permutation matching the simple factors up to isomorphism.

items.title: The order of a finite group is the product of the orders of its composition factors
items.strategy: Apply the finite quotient-cardinality formula at every adjacent normal inclusion in a composition series and telescope. Mention the trivial group, whose empty product is 1.

items.title: Characteristic subgroups
Characteristic subgroups are normal, and characteristicity is transitive
items.strategy: Inner automorphisms show H char G implies H◁G. If K char H char G, every automorphism of G restricts to an automorphism of H and hence preserves K, proving K char G. Keep separate the false mixed assertion K◁H char G⇒K◁G, which is tested on the companion page.

items.title: The derived subgroup is characteristic and the abelianization is universal
items.strategy: Automorphisms preserve commutators, so they preserve [G,G]; characteristicity supplies normality without appealing to the existing AI-authored normality proof. Use the published quotient-abelian criterion and quotient universal property to prove that every homomorphism G→A into an abelian group factors uniquely through G^ab=G/[G,G].

items.title: The derived series, solvable groups, and derived length
Homomorphisms respect commutator subgroups and derived series
items.strategy: Compute f([x,y])=[f(x),f(y)] to obtain f(G')≤f(G)' and equality when f is surjective. Induct on r to obtain f(G^(r))≤f(G)^(r), again with equality for surjections; specialize to inclusions and quotient maps.

items.title: A group is solvable if and only if it has a subnormal series with abelian factors
items.strategy: If the derived series reaches 1, its successive factors are abelian. Conversely, for G=G_0▷⋯▷G_n=1 with abelian factors, quotient abelianness gives G_i'≤G_{i+1}; inductively G^(i)≤G_i, so G^(n)=1. This also shows the derived series is the fastest descending abelian-factor series.

items.title: Subgroups and quotients of solvable groups are solvable
items.strategy: For H≤G use H^(r)≤G^(r), and for a quotient use surjectivity to identify the quotient's r-th derived subgroup with the image of G^(r). Termination of the derived series then descends in both cases, without a finiteness hypothesis.

items.title: Extensions and finite direct products of solvable groups are solvable
items.strategy: For N◁G with N and G/N solvable, choose r with (G/N)^(r)=1, infer G^(r)≤N, then choose s with N^(s)=1 and show G^(r+s)≤N^(s). Prove (G×H)'=G'×H' directly from coordinate commutators and iterate; derive the finite-product statement by induction.

items.title: A finite group is solvable if and only if all its composition factors are cyclic of prime order
items.strategy: A simple solvable group has nontrivial last derived quotient and must be abelian; a finite simple abelian group is cyclic of prime order by Cauchy's theorem. Thus solvability passes to every composition factor. Conversely, rebuild the group along a composition series using the extension theorem, since prime-order factors are abelian and solvable.

items.title: $A_5$ and $S_n$ for $n\ge5$ are not solvable
items.strategy: Use the published simplicity of A_5 and the published equality A_5'=A_5 to show its derived series never reaches 1. For n≥5, embed A_5 into S_n by fixing the remaining letters; a solvable S_n would have only solvable subgroups, contradiction. Also note directly that A_n is nonsolvable for every n≥5 from the published derived-subgroup computation.

items.title: Subgroup commutators and the lower central series
The upper central series
Nilpotent groups and nilpotency class
Central factors are equivalent to adjacent commutator containments
items.strategy: For N◁G and N≤H≤G, prove H/N≤Z(G/N) iff [G,H]≤N by expanding the quotient commutator. Apply this equivalence to each adjacent pair in a normal series; include the endpoint cases N=1 and H=G explicitly.

items.title: Nilpotence via central series, the upper central series, and the lower central series
items.strategy: Show every central series of length c lies termwise below the upper central series and termwise above the reversed lower central series, using the commutator criterion. Hence Z_c(G)=G iff γ_{c+1}(G)=1 iff G admits a central series of length c; take the least such c to identify nilpotency class.

items.title: Subgroups, quotients, and finite direct products of nilpotent groups are nilpotent
items.strategy: For H≤G, inductively prove γ_r(H)≤γ_r(G). For a quotient map q, prove q(γ_r(G))=γ_r(G/N). For a product, compute γ_r(G×H)=γ_r(G)×γ_r(H) from coordinate commutators. Termination gives the three closure results and the expected maximum bound on product class.

items.title: Every finite $p$-group is nilpotent
items.strategy: Induct on |G|. The published nontrivial-center theorem gives 1≠Z(G); the quotient G/Z(G) is a smaller finite p-group and hence nilpotent. Pull its upper central series back through the quotient map and prepend 1≤Z(G), obtaining an upper central series for G. Treat the trivial group separately.

items.title: Nilpotent groups, and in particular finite $p$-groups, are solvable
items.strategy: Use [H,H]≤[G,H] to prove G^(r)≤γ_{r+1}(G) by induction, so lower-central termination implies derived-series termination. Apply the finite-p-group theorem. This supplies a large, explicit family of solvable groups of small order without importing the later Sylow theory.

items.title: A central extension of a class-$c$ nilpotent group is nilpotent of class at most $c+1$
items.strategy: If N≤Z(G) and G/N has lower-central length c, quotient functoriality gives γ_{c+1}(G)≤N. Centrality then gives γ_{c+2}(G)=[G,γ_{c+1}(G)]≤[G,N]=1. Record that arbitrary extensions of nilpotent groups need not be nilpotent, as the S_3 companion counterexample shows.

title: Conjugacy in $S_n$, Generation, and the Simplicity of $A_n$

items.title: Conjugating a cycle relabels each entry: $g(a_1\,\ldots\,a_k)g^{-1}=(g(a_1)\,\ldots\,g(a_k))$
items.strategy: Evaluate the conjugate at each relabelled cycle point and at every point outside their set. The first calculation advances one position and the second fixes the point, which proves equality as permutations rather than merely agreement on the displayed support.

items.title: Two elements of $S_n$ are conjugate if and only if they have the same cycle type
items.strategy: Conjugate a disjoint-cycle decomposition factor by factor using the relabelling lemma, proving invariance of cycle type. Conversely align equally long cycles, including fixed points, and define one bijection sending their entries positionwise; the same lemma shows it conjugates the first permutation to the second.

items.title: The conjugacy classes of $S_n$ are indexed by the tuples $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ with $\sum k c_k=n$
items.strategy: The cycle-type definition gives exactly one such multiplicity tuple for each permutation, and the conjugacy classification says two permutations give the same tuple exactly when they lie in the same conjugacy class. Construct a representative from disjoint cycles for every admissible tuple, including $n=0$.

items.title: If $\sigma\in S_n$ has $c_k$ cycles of length $k$, then $|C_{S_n}(\sigma)|=\prod_{k=1}^n k^{c_k}c_k!$
items.strategy: A commuting permutation must send each $\langle\sigma\rangle$-orbit to another orbit of the same length. For the $c_k$ length-$k$ orbits, choose an arbitrary permutation of those orbits and an independent cyclic offset on each, giving $c_k!k^{c_k}$ choices; prove these choices assemble uniquely and multiply independently across lengths. Check $c_k=0$, the identity, and $n=0$ via empty products.

items.title: The class equation of $S_n$ is $n!=\sum_{\sum k c_k=n} n!/\prod_k k^{c_k}c_k!$
items.strategy: Index the conjugacy classes by cycle-type tuples, combine conjugacy-class cardinality with the centralizer formula, and sum the disjoint class sizes. At $n=0$ the single empty type contributes $1$.

items.title: $Z(S_n)$ is trivial for $n\ge3$
items.strategy: A central permutation has a singleton conjugacy class, hence its cycle type has class-size formula $1$. Show every nonidentity cycle type for $n\ge3$ has more than one relabelling, or directly choose a transposition whose conjugation changes a moved point; conclude only the identity is central. Record the exceptional abelian groups $S_0,S_1,S_2$.

items.title: The adjacent transpositions $(1\,2),(2\,3),\ldots,(n-1\,n)$ generate $S_n$
items.strategy: Express every transposition $(a\,b)$ with $a<b$ as the standard palindromic word in adjacent transpositions, checking the word pointwise. Since all transpositions generate $S_n$, so do the adjacent ones; include $n=0,1$ as empty generating sets for the trivial groups.

items.title: For $n\ge2$, $(1\,2\,\ldots\,n)$ and $(1\,2)$ generate $S_n$
items.strategy: Conjugating $(1\,2)$ by successive powers of the $n$-cycle produces every neighboring transposition around the cycle, in particular the standard adjacent transpositions. Apply adjacent generation; at $n=2$ the two displayed generators coincide and still generate $S_2$.

items.title: $A_n$ is generated by $3$-cycles for every $n\ge3$
items.strategy: Write an even permutation as a product of an even number of transpositions and pair them. Equal pairs cancel, overlapping pairs are one $3$-cycle, and disjoint pairs are a product of two $3$-cycles by explicit identities; hence every even permutation lies in the subgroup generated by $3$-cycles, while every $3$-cycle is even.

items.title: A conjugacy class in an index-two normal subgroup remains one class or splits into two equal classes, with a centralizer criterion
items.strategy: For $H\trianglelefteq G$ of index two and $x\in H$, write $G=H\sqcup tH$. Then $\operatorname{Cl}_G(x)$ is the union of the $H$-class of $x$ and its $t$-conjugate. The two classes agree exactly when some element outside $H$ centralizes $x$; otherwise they are disjoint and conjugation by $t$ bijects them, giving equal size.

items.title: An $S_n$-class of an even permutation splits in $A_n$ exactly when all cycle lengths, including $1$-cycles, are odd and distinct
items.strategy: Use the index-two splitting lemma with $H=A_n$. An even-length cycle is itself an odd centralizer element; two equal odd-length cycles can be swapped by an odd permutation, including two fixed points. Conversely, when the lengths are distinct and odd, every centralizer element preserves each cycle support and restricts there to a power of that odd cycle, hence is even. This proves both directions and the equal-size conclusion.

items.title: All $3$-cycles are conjugate in $A_n$ for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: They have common cycle type $(3,1^{n-3})$. The splitting criterion does not split that type when $n\ge5$ because the fixed-point length $1$ is repeated; equivalently correct an odd $S_n$ conjugator by a transposition on two fixed points.

items.title: Simple groups
A normal subgroup of $A_n$ containing one $3$-cycle equals $A_n$ for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Normality contains the whole $A_n$-conjugacy class of the given $3$-cycle. All $3$-cycles form that one class for $n\ge5$, and the separate generation theorem says they generate $A_n$.

items.title: Every nontrivial normal subgroup of $A_n$ contains a $3$-cycle for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Choose a nonidentity element of the normal subgroup with maximal number of fixed points. If it is not a $3$-cycle, split its cycle structure into the two exhaustive regimes: it has a cycle of length at least three with additional moved points, or it is a product of disjoint transpositions. In each regime choose a $3$-cycle $g$ so the nonidentity commutator $g\sigma g^{-1}\sigma^{-1}$ lies in the subgroup but fixes strictly more points, a contradiction. Verify separately the $4$-cycle and two-transposition edge configurations and the availability of a fifth point.

items.title: $A_n$ is simple for every $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Let $N\trianglelefteq A_n$. If $N$ is nontrivial, the preceding support-reduction lemma supplies a $3$-cycle, and the normal-subgroup lemma then gives $N=A_n$. Exhibit two noncommuting $3$-cycles to ensure $A_n$ is nontrivial and nonabelian under the stated convention for simple groups.

items.title: For $n\ge5$, the only proper nontrivial normal subgroup of $S_n$ is $A_n$
items.strategy: For $N\trianglelefteq S_n$, simplicity makes $N\cap A_n$ either trivial or all of $A_n$. The latter gives $N=A_n$ or $S_n$; in the former case sign is injective on $N$, so a nontrivial $N$ has order two and its unique nonidentity element is central in $S_n$, contradicting triviality of the center.

items.title: $[S_n,S_n]=A_n$ for $n\ge2$, and $[A_n,A_n]=A_n$ for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Because sign has abelian image, the quotient criterion puts $[S_n,S_n]$ inside $A_n$; every $3$-cycle is an explicit commutator of transpositions, so $3$-cycle generation gives the reverse inclusion. For $A_n$, its commutator subgroup is normal; two overlapping $3$-cycles do not commute, so it is nontrivial, and simplicity forces it to be all of $A_n$.

title: Frattini Subgroups and the Burnside Basis Theorem — Examples

items.title: The Frattini subgroup of a nontrivial cyclic $p$-group
items.strategy: For $P=\langle g\rangle$ of order $p^n$ with $n\ge1$, use the cyclic power-order formula to identify $P^p=\langle g^p\rangle$ and use commutativity to set $P'=1$. The Frattini formula gives $\Phi(P)=\langle g^p\rangle$, the quotient has order $p$, and its one-element basis gives $d(P)=1$. Check $n=1$ separately.

items.title: The Frattini subgroup of $(\mathbb Z/p)^n$ is trivial
items.strategy: With componentwise addition, $(\mathbb Z/p)^n$ is elementary abelian, including the empty product at $n=0$. The Frattini-free characterization gives $\Phi((\mathbb Z/p)^n)=1$. The coordinate vectors form a basis in the native finite $\mathbb F_p$ sense, so the generator rank is $n$.

items.title: The Frattini subgroups of the dihedral and quaternion groups of order eight
items.strategy: Use the semidirect-product normal forms for $D_8=\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$ to compute $D_8'=D_8^2=\langle r^2\rangle$. In $Q_8$, the quaternion multiplication table gives $Q_8'=Q_8^2=\{\pm1\}$. The finite-two-group formula yields both Frattini subgroups; in each case the quotient is $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$ and the generator rank is two.

items.title: The $3\times3$ upper-unitriangular group over a prime field has generator rank two
items.strategy: For each prime $p$, construct $H_p=(\mathbb Z/p)^3$ with $(a,b,c)(a',b',c')=(a+a',b+b',c+c'+ab')$ and verify associativity, identity, inverses, and order $p^3$. Direct commutator calculation gives $H_p'=\{(0,0,c)\}$; for odd $p$ all $p$th powers are trivial, while for $p=2$ every square lies on the same central axis. The Frattini formula therefore gives $\Phi(H_p)=\{(0,0,c)\}$, and the first two coordinate classes form a basis of the quotient. This includes $p=2$ without assuming exponent $p$.

items.title: The maximal subgroups of the dihedral group of order eight as Frattini hyperplanes
items.strategy: For $D_8=\langle r,s\rangle$ from the preceding example, list the three maximal subgroups $\langle r\rangle$, $\langle r^2,s\rangle$, and $\langle r^2,rs\rangle$. Modulo $\Phi(D_8)=\langle r^2\rangle$, identify them with the three one-dimensional subgroups of $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$ and write the three nonzero coordinate-sum homomorphisms whose kernels they are.

items.title: A nonsurjective homomorphism need not carry the Frattini subgroup into the target Frattini subgroup
items.strategy: Embed $C_4=\langle g\rangle$ in $S_5$ by sending $g$ to $(1\,2\,3\,4)$. The cyclic example gives $\Phi(C_4)=\langle g^2\rangle$, whose image contains the nonidentity double transposition $(1\,3)(2\,4)$. The Frattini subgroup of $S_5$ is nilpotent and normal; the normal-subgroup classification leaves $1,A_5,S_5$, and the latter two are not solvable and hence not nilpotent, so $\Phi(S_5)=1$. Thus the image inclusion fails, while surjectivity remains the exact valid hypothesis.

items.title: The Fitting subgroup of $A_5$ does not contain its centralizer
items.strategy: The Fitting subgroup is normal and nilpotent. Simplicity of $A_5$ makes it either $1$ or $A_5$; the second option would make $A_5$ nilpotent and therefore solvable, contradicting the published nonsolvability theorem. Hence $F(A_5)=1$, so $C_{A_5}(F(A_5))=A_5\nleq1$. This isolates the solvability hypothesis in the published self-centralization theorem.

items.title: Inversion on $C_3$ is detected on its Frattini quotient
items.strategy: The cyclic example gives $\Phi(C_3)=1$. Inversion is a nonidentity automorphism of order two, coprime to three, and its induced action on $C_3/\Phi(C_3)=C_3$ is still inversion. This concrete action illustrates the Hall–Burnside conclusion and checks that the theorem does not claim such automorphisms are absent, only that their quotient action is faithful.

items.title: FALSE: the Frattini subgroup is the union of the maximal subgroups
items.strategy: In $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$, the Frattini subgroup is trivial, while every nonzero vector spans one of the three maximal order-two subgroups. Their union is the whole four-element group. Thus union and intersection differ maximally in this example.

items.title: FALSE: every homomorphism carries the Frattini subgroup into the target Frattini subgroup
items.strategy: Invoke the preceding explicit embedding $C_4\hookrightarrow S_5$: its image of $\Phi(C_4)$ is nontrivial while $\Phi(S_5)=1$. State the valid surjective-image inclusion separately and identify nonsurjectivity as the missing hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: all minimal generating sets of a finite group have the same size
items.strategy: In the additive cyclic group $\mathbb Z/6$, the singleton $\{1\}$ is a minimal generating set, while $\{2,3\}$ also generates and neither singleton does. Hence the two inclusion-minimal generating sets have different sizes; the finite-$p$ hypothesis in Burnside basis cannot be removed.

items.title: FALSE: the Fitting subgroup always contains its centralizer
items.strategy: Use the preceding $A_5$ computation: $F(A_5)=1$ and $C_{A_5}(F(A_5))=A_5$. Contrast it with the published theorem for finite solvable groups, identifying solvability as the missing hypothesis.
